lesson.title: How Big Is an Atom? Measuring the Immeasurable
lesson.summary: Atomic radius shrinks across a period and grows down a group, a pattern that falls directly out of the effective nuclear charge tug of war and gives chemists a simple way to compare atom sizes.
lesson.body:
Atoms do not have hard, billiard ball edges. An electron's probability cloud technically extends outward without ever truly reaching zero, so there is no single sharp boundary chemists can point to and call the edge of an atom. In practice, atomic radius is defined operationally instead: usually as half the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together, a covalent radius, or packed next to each other in a solid metal, a metallic radius. It is a measured, comparative quantity rather than a geometrically exact one, but it is remarkably consistent and useful precisely because it is measured the same way across the whole table.

The trend in atomic radius falls directly out of the effective nuclear charge tug of war introduced in the periodic trends chapter. Moving across a period, protons are added to the nucleus while electrons are added to the same outer shell, so effective nuclear charge climbs steadily and pulls the valence electrons in tighter, shrinking the atom. Moving down a group, each new period adds an entirely new, larger principal energy level, and the added shielding from that much bigger core of inner electrons outweighs the modest rise in effective nuclear charge, so the atom expands.

Period 3 shows the across-a-period shrinkage clearly, with atomic radii falling steadily from sodium to chlorine: sodium about 186 pm, magnesium about 160 pm, aluminum about 143 pm, silicon about 117 pm, phosphorus about 110 pm, sulfur about 104 pm, and chlorine about 99 pm. That is nearly a factor of two reduction across just seven elements, driven entirely by adding protons to a nucleus whose shielding core, the filled 1s2 2s2 2p6 electrons, never grows.

Group 1 shows the down-a-group growth just as clearly: lithium about 152 pm, sodium about 186 pm, potassium about 227 pm, rubidium about 248 pm, and cesium about 265 pm. Cesium's nucleus, with 55 protons, exerts a vastly larger pull than lithium's 3 protons, yet cesium is nearly twice as large, because its lone valence electron sits all the way out in the sixth principal shell, shielded by four complete inner shells that lithium simply does not have.

A couple of honest caveats are worth knowing. Noble gases are often measured differently, using van der Waals radius rather than covalent radius, since they rarely form ordinary bonds to measure a distance between. Transition metals also show a flatter, less dramatic shrinkage across their rows than main group elements do, because added electrons go into inner d orbitals that shield the outer valence electrons fairly effectively, partly offsetting the added nuclear charge. Even with those nuances, atomic radius remains one of the most useful single numbers in chemistry, correlating with everything from density and melting point to how readily an atom loses or gains electrons, the exact question tackled next in ionic radius.
